title: The Puratan tradition
hookLine: one old family of janamsakhis, valued by historians for its early material

cards: An old house, renovated many times. New kitchen, new windows, a porch someone added. But go down to the basement and there's a stretch of stone wall, rough and uneven, from when the house was first built.

A builder will run a hand along it and say: that's the original. Everything else rests on it. There isn't one janamsakhi but several families of them, and historians go looking for the stone wall in the basement.

teach.b: Puratan is a Punjabi word for old.

teach.h: A FAMILY OF MANUSCRIPTS, NOT ONE BOOK.
teach.b: This family of janamsakhis carries that name, the old ones, and historians value it for its early material about Guru Nanak's life. It isn't one book with one author.
It's a group of related manuscripts telling the stories in much the same way. Some readers describe it as plainer than later tellings.
The stories are spare and move quickly, with less decoration around them, and the Guru's own hymns are woven into the scenes. Take the river story, one of the pictures from yesterday's opening.

Nanak goes down to the river to bathe and doesn't come back. His family and friends search, and fear the worst. When he returns, the Puratan tradition has him say: there is no Hindu, there is no Musalman.

Sikh teachers often explain those words as a call to look past the labels people fight over, toward the One who made them all, not a rejection of anyone's faith. A historian reading that story isn't trying to disprove it.
They're asking a different question: which parts of the telling are oldest, closest to the people who knew Nanak, and which grew around it later?
The Puratan tradition is where historians often start that work.
And calling something the old telling doesn't make the later tellings worthless. A renovated house is still a home. But when you want to know how the house began, you go to the stone.

how: Scholars of Sikh history read the Puratan janamsakhis alongside other traditions, while gurdwara teachers draw sakhis such as the river story from them for katha and for children.

practice: Choose someone you've known a long time, a parent, a friend, a place you've lived, and go past everything you know about them today, back to the very first picture you have: where you stood, the light, what was said.
That first picture is the stone wall; notice how much has been built on it since, and that it's still there, holding it up. If you pray, you can say Waheguru when you reach it.
